t:
(a) Expansion of Authority to Energy Resiliency and Energy Security Projects.—
        (1) In general.—Section 2914 of title 10, United States Code, is amended—
            (A) in the section heading, by inserting “resiliency and” before “conservation construction projects”; and 
            (B) in subsection (a), by striking “military construction project for energy conservation” and inserting “military construction project for energy resiliency, energy security, or energy conservation”.  
        (2) Clerical amendment.—The table of sections at the beginning of chapter 173 of such title is amended by striking the item relating to section 2914 and inserting the following new item:

“2914. 
Energy resiliency and conservation construction projects.”.

  
    (b) Notice and Reporting Requirements for Projects.—
        (1) Contents of notifications.—
            (A) Contents.—Section 2914(b) of title 10, United States Code, is amended—
                (i) by striking “When a decision” and inserting “(1) When a decision”; and 
                (ii) by adding at the end the following new paragraph:“(2) The Secretary of Defense shall include in each notification submitted under paragraph (1) the following information:“(A) In the case of a military construction project for energy conservation, the justification and current cost estimate for the project, the expected savings-to-investment ratio, simple payback estimates, and the project’s measurement and verification cost estimate.“(B) In the case of a military construction project for energy resiliency or energy security, the rationale for how the project would enhance mission assurance, support mission critical functions, and address known vulnerabilities.”.  
            (B) Effective date.—The amendment made by subparagraph (A) shall apply with respect to notifications provided during fiscal year 2017 or any succeeding fiscal year.  
        (2) Annual report.—Section 2914 of such title is amended by adding at the end the following new subsection:“(c) Annual Report.—Not later than 90 days after the end of each fiscal year (beginning with fiscal year 2017), the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the appropriate committees of Congress a report on the status of the planned and active projects carried out under this section (including completed projects), and shall include in the report with respect to each such project the following information:“(1) The title, location, a brief description of the scope of work, the original project cost estimate, and the current working cost estimate.“(2) In the case of a military construction project for energy conservation—“(A) the original expected savings-to-investment ratio and simple payback estimates and measurement and verification cost estimate;“(B) the most current expected savings-to-investment ratio and simple payback estimates and measurement and verification plan and costs; and“(C) a brief description of the measurement and verification plan and planned funding source.“(3) In the case of a military construction project for energy resiliency or energy security, the rationale for how the project would enhance mission assurance, support mission critical functions, and address known vulnerabilities.“(4) Such other information as the Secretary considers appropriate.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the notice and annual reporting requirements are a form of participation. They are not, because the notifications and reports go only to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. The rest of the section just expands military construction authority to energy resiliency and security projects, with no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue involving any outside party.
fable.s: the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the appropriate committees of Congress a report on the status of the planned and active projects carried out under this section

opus.w: The section widens the military construction authority to include energy resiliency and energy security projects, and adds notice and annual reporting requirements. All of those notices and reports go from the Secretary of Defense to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government. Reports and notices to Congress look procedural, but they never bring a non-federal party into a federal decision. The section has no comment period, rulemaking, hearing, outside advisory body, outside consultation or right to sue.
opus.s: the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the appropriate committees of Congress a report on the status of the planned and active projects carried out under this section
opus.b: **Step 1: The tempting reading.** The section is full of procedure: notifications with required contents and an annual report on each project. It could look like participation. But every notification and report goes from the Secretary of Defense to "the appropriate committees of Congress." Congress is inside the federal government. No state, tribe, company, expert or member of the public is consulted, and nobody outside the government gets a right to sue or object. The section fails the gate.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Secretary of Defense to submit reports and notifications to congressional committees. Congress is part of the federal government, so this is intra-governmental communication, not participation with outside parties. There is no requirement for public comment, consultation with states or tribes, or involvement of non-federal advisory bodies.
qwen_chat.s: The Secretary of Defense shall submit to the appropriate committees of Congress a report on the status of the planned and active projects carried out under this section
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the "notice" requirements in subsection (b)(1) constitute participation because they involve notifying someone about a decision. However, the text specifies that these notifications are submitted to "the appropriate committees of Congress" (as seen in the parallel reporting requirement in (b)(2) and standard statutory context for such military construction notifications). Congress is inside the federal government. Therefore, notifying Congress is intra-governmental communication, not participation with outside parties. There is no mention of public comment periods, advisory boards with non-federal members, or consultation with states/tribes/public.
